In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill [for a third time](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/). The bill will now go to the Senate for their consideration. Unfortunately, the parliamentary library has not (yet?) produced a parliamentary digest on this bill, which is usually the best source of non-partisan information on bills. The majority voted against an [amendment](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2021-11-25.37.1) to a motion, which means it failed. ### Amendment text > *At the end of the motion, add "and, in respect of the [Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fbillhome%2Fr6802%22), the provisions of the bill be referred immediately to the Economics Legislation Committee for inquiry and report by 24 March 2022".*

The Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 was moved to require active consent from class action members, cap funder and lawyer shares at 30% of proceeds, and mandate court approval of distributions to ensure fair returns for claimants, citing cases like Banksia Securities and Wittenbury v Vocation where funders and lawyers took nearly 50% of settlements.

The speaker argued the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 is Orwellian and will harm ordinary Australians' access to justice, citing a 30 per cent cap on costs and a switch to opt-in class actions as design features that benefit defendants. He announced Labor will oppose the bill and move a second reading amendment, referencing the robodebt scheme (430,000 victims, $1.7 billion restitution) and an underpaid Aboriginal wages case as examples of class actions that would be prevented.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 is needed to regulate litigation funders and ensure class action members receive at least 70% of claim proceeds, with a rebuttable presumption against non-member distributions exceeding 30%. The bill responds to Australian Law Reform Commission findings showing median plaintiff returns drop from 85% (without funders) to 51% (with funders), and to a parliamentary committee’s 31 recommendations.

The Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 would restrict access to class actions for many Australians, particularly victims of financial fraud like those from the Trio Capital collapse, by imposing court approval requirements and a rebuttable presumption that distributions under 70% to plaintiffs are unfair. The bill was criticised for its rushed inquiry process, which gave the public only days to respond, and for potentially discouraging settlements, increasing costs, and benefiting wealthy defendants over ordinary plaintiffs.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 addresses the free rider problem in open class actions by establishing a new managed investment scheme for litigation funding and requiring fair and reasonable returns to funders, based on recommendations from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Corporations and Financial Services and the Australian Law Reform Commission.

The speaker opposed the Corporations Amendment Bill, arguing that class actions are the only means of redress for people harmed by government and corporate actions—citing Queensland taxi owners, stolen wages for Indigenous Australians, and the live cattle export ban—and warned of personal retaliation against those who destroy livelihoods.

The speech supported the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021, arguing that litigation funders exploit vulnerable plaintiffs by taking large shares of court-awarded compensation. It argued for stronger regulation and court oversight of litigation funding contracts while affirming that class actions remain legal.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 is a deceptive attempt by the Morrison-Joyce government to protect wealthy defendants by making class actions harder for everyday Australians, contrary to its stated consumer protection purpose. They cited opposition from the Law Council, Phi Finney McDonald, and defendant lawyers at Herbert Smith Freehills, and noted constitutional concerns raised by Justice Beach and former Solicitor-General Justin Gleeson SC, as well as specific class actions—including stolen wages, stolen generations, Westpac overcharging, PFAS contamination, and Domino’s underpayment cases—that would not have proceeded under the bill.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment Bill 2021 would harm access to justice by making class actions harder, citing that community legal centres turn away over 160,000 people annually and that the bill would have required 430,000 robodebt class action members to opt in. The speaker announced Labor's opposition to the bill.

The speaker opposed the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021, arguing it would restrict class actions by requiring court approval for funding agreements over 30% and shifting from an opt-out to an opt-in system, thereby making it harder for ordinary Australians, particularly remote and Indigenous communities, to access justice.

The speaker argued the bill is misleadingly titled and will actually hinder access to justice by protecting wealthy defendants, citing constitutional concerns, a rushed and inadequate consultation process, and examples of landmark class actions—such as stolen wages and environmental contamination cases—that would be blocked under its measures.

The speaker opposed the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021, arguing it would harm access to justice by making class actions harder to bring. They cited examples such as a $500 million settlement for 2009 Victorian bushfire survivors, a $112 million robodebt class action for 450,000 people, and actions against major banks and Sigma Pharmaceuticals, and noted concerns from legal expert Justin Gleeson that the bill may be unconstitutional.

The speaker opposed the 30% cap on litigation funder fees in the Corporations Amendment Bill, arguing it would reduce access to justice for small businesses and individuals by altering funders' risk-reward calculations. He cited high legal costs, a defamation case costing nearly $2 million without trial, and discrepancies between TGA and AusVaxSafety data on COVID vaccine adverse events.

The speaker opposed the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021, arguing it would replace the opt-out class action model with an opt-in requirement and flawed fund distribution rules, making class actions harder for ordinary Australians while protecting large corporations. They urged the government to withdraw or vote against the bill.

The speaker supported the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021, arguing it would ensure class action claimants receive a fairer share of damages by capping litigation funders’ take at 30% and citing cases where claimants received as little as 33% of settlements.

The speaker argued the bill makes justice harder for ordinary Australians, citing expert John Sheahan's view that it "makes things worse for everyone." They opposed the 70-30 cost split and opt-in requirement, claiming these will block meritorious claims and protect large corporate defendants, while criticizing the rushed three-week committee process and lack of a proper regulatory impact statement.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021 would fundamentally weaken class actions by shifting from an opt-out to an opt-in structure, denying access to justice for vulnerable people, especially in rural, regional and remote communities. They also criticised the bill's process as atrocious and biased, and claimed it was possibly unconstitutional and driven by ideology rather than evidence.

Craig Kelly moved amendments to the Corporations Amendment (Improving Outcomes for Litigation Funding Participants) Bill 2021, proposing a discretionary triple-damages provision for Australian Consumer Law contraventions modelled on US antitrust law, and stated he would not support the bill unless the amendments passed.

The majority voted in favour of [government amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2018-09-11.4.2) (1) to (5) and (8) to (11), which means they succeeded. ### What do these amendments do? These amendments would move several matters that are currently in disallowable instruments - that is, legislative instruments that the parliament is able to vote against in a single vote so they stop being law - to standard legislation that can't so easily be undone. These matters include the location of the trial sites. According to Liberal MP [Mitch Fifield](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/victoria/mitch_fifield), who introduced the amendments, *"[this will give certainty](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2018-09-11.6.1) to trial participants and local communities"*. ### What does the bill do? The [bill was introduced to](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6130): * *expand the cashless debit card arrangements to a further trial site, the Bundaberg and Hervey Bay area, to run until 30 June 2020;* * *specify the class of trial participants for the area and increase the total number of trial participants overall to 15 000;* * *provide for an exception from the restrictive trade practices provisions of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 for merchants that implement product level blocking systems to identify that a cashless debit card is being used for payment and, if any restricted products are being purchased, decline the transaction; and* * *limit the use of the restricted portion of a payment to prevent the portion being used to obtain cash-like products which could be used to obtain alcohol or gambling.*

Labor opposed the expansion of the cashless debit card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, citing community opposition from both local mayors, a lack of formal consultation, an inconclusive and poor-quality ORIMA evaluation, and program costs exceeding $24 million to date (including $7.9 million paid to Indue and $1.6 million to ORIMA). It committed to supporting the current trials in Ceduna and the East Kimberley until mid-2019, but would only consider new sites with credible evidence of effectiveness and an agreed community consultation process and definition of consent.

The speaker argued for the expansion of the Cashless Debit Card trial to the Hinkler electorate, citing strong community support, over 188 consultation meetings, a ReachTEL poll showing 27.8% opposition, and a cost of less than $2,000 per person. They invited the member for Barton to meet frontline service providers rather than union officials, and noted that the trial would affect 6,700 participants on specific welfare payments to address child neglect and gambling-related harm.

The speaker argued for expanding the Cashless Debit Card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, citing independent evaluation results showing reduced alcohol and drug use, gambling, and improved savings and childcare in existing trial sites (Ceduna and East Kimberley). The bill extends the trial to about 6,700 welfare recipients under 36 in those areas, with additional $1 million in community services, and amends the list of restricted goods to include cash-like products.

The member for Herbert opposed the cashless debit card trial expansion, arguing it should not be imposed on communities that reject it, and instead advocated for early intervention and prevention programs, citing a $5 million commitment to a Salvation Army detox facility and noting that 78% of trial participants reported little or no change.

The speaker opposed the bill to expand the cashless debit card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, arguing the government failed to properly consult communities and lacked credible evidence. They noted the expansion would add around 6,700 participants, bringing the total to over 15,000, and criticised the $1.6 million ORIMA evaluation as unreliable while highlighting the $24 million spent on existing trials.

The bill expands the cashless debit card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, covering around 6,700 people under 36 on Newstart, youth allowance, or parenting payments, running until 30 June 2020, based on community consultation and evidence of intergenerational welfare dependency.

The speaker argued against expanding the Cashless Debit Card trial to Bundaberg and Hervey Bay, citing a woeful evaluation, no reduction in violence, and a damning Auditor-General's report, while supporting continuation of existing trials in Ceduna and East Kimberley for two years. They opposed the national rollout, insisting on genuine community consultation and wraparound services instead of mandatory income management.

The bill would create a commission that investigates misconduct in Australia's banking and finance industry.
This commission would report its findings to the Parliament, using powers like legal cross-examination and forensic analysis.
The bill would start only after royal assent and when government funds are available to pay for the inquiry.
Establishes a parliamentary commission to examine banking and finance misconduct.
Requires the commission to identify causes like flawed incentives, culture and weak regulation.
Delays commencement until both royal assent and funding from the Consolidated Revenue Fund occur.

Banks, insurance companies, superannuation funds, credit providers, financial advisors and other financial services license holders would be examined, and victims of misconduct would have their experiences considered.

Adam Bandt I move: That this bill be now read a second time. We need a royal commission into the big banks, and the best way to make this happen is to vote for this bill, because we will either then get a royal commission, when the government realises that there is support both in the Senate and in this House for a royal commission into the big banks, or we will get the next best thing, which is a parliamentary commission of inquiry that will have the power to do what a royal commission can. This bill is very similar in its terms to that moved by my colleague the member for Kennedy and seconded by the member for Denison. There is a broad-based support for this approach in this chamber. There is a broad-based support for this in the Senate. That is why this bill that the Greens have drafted was co-sponsored and moved by a broad cross-section of the Senate. Too many people have lost too much money. There have been homes that have been lost, there have been farms that have been lost, and there have been lives that have been wrecked. At its core, the problem is that within the banks there is a conflict in their business model. Part of their business model takes people's money and invests it, but the other part of their business model is about making as much money as they possibly can. Those two often come into conflict. This parliament has tried its best to inquire into what is going on in the big banks and whether we can fix it. There have been Senate inquiries. The House economics committee has looked into this. Each time, what we find is that the CEOs of the banks front up to parliament and wring their hands and say, 'We're sorry that we've done the wrong thing.' But we find out that back at the ranch—when they leave parliament and go back to running their businesses—nothing, fundamentally, changes.
